barriers.description: There were no suitable off-the-shelf measurement interfaces, and budget and time constraints forced the team to develop an early prototype in-house.
barriers.justification: Lack of available hardware and limited funding/time constrained the team's ability to procure existing tools, increasing workload for producing design solutions and slowing iteration and evaluation activities.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Design of an early prototype for palpation training was planned due to a lack of available oﬀ-the-shelf measurement interfaces with the ﬂexibility required for this study. Moreover, additional factors such as budget restrictions and time commitments were inﬂuential in making this decision.

barriers.description: End users were not available for early evaluation, so proxies (colleagues) were used instead to run Cognitive Walkthroughs.
barriers.justification: Unavailability of real end-users limited authentic user involvement and evaluation, reducing the team's ability to manage evolving user understanding and to integrate user feedback effectively in early iterations.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Cognitive Walkthrough was used to evaluate the early prototype, when an end-user is not available with the help of proxies (e.g. fellow colleagues) to ensure it complies with the domain principles which were extracted via literature reviews and process observations.

barriers.description: Ethnographic field methods were considered infeasible because they are costly and time-consuming, preventing long-term embedded observations.
barriers.justification: The inability to perform extended ethnographic studies limited the team's capacity to deeply understand real training contexts and constrained the 'understand context of use' and 'manage user understanding' workloads.
barriers.reference_excerpt: ethnography (or ﬁeld study) is one of the most eﬀective methods in ergonomics studies to determine challenges and collect information about conventional practice. However, it is a costly and time consuming method in which the investigator is physically involved/embedded in the whole training programme (in medical school) for long-term investigations.

barriers.description: Only four senior clinical tutors were involved in developing the ground-truth model, and the authors state more expert collaboration was required.
barriers.justification: Limited expert participation constrained the team's ability to produce a robust, generalisable best-practice model and hindered specifying reliable user requirements and validating assessment criteria.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Four senior clinical tutors were involved in order to develop a ground theory in a limited timeframe and more collaboration from experts are required to improve eﬃciency and reliability of the proposed approach.

barriers.description: Recruitment difficulties and participant withdrawals reduced representation across body types and genders (e.g., no large female volunteers; a male withdrew prior to data collection).
barriers.justification: Restricted access to diverse actor patients limited the team's ability to understand context-of-use variability and to create an averaged anatomy model, hindering evaluation and generalisability of findings.
barriers.reference_excerpt: It was diﬃcult to ﬁnd a female participant in the Large category as no one within that category volunteered and it was deemed unethical to ask individuals directly. Just prior to the start of the data collection, the male participant in the medium body category withdrew.

barriers.description: Institutional permissions limited changes to room layout, restricting where the TFT display could be placed during experiments.
barriers.justification: Restricted room/setting permissions prevented designing ideal real-world evaluation setups and constrained evaluation and user involvement practices (e.g., positioning feedback displays close to patients), reducing ecological validity of tests.
barriers.reference_excerpt: The investigator had limited permissions to change the room settings to position the TFT display next to the patient’s face.

barriers.description: Current sensing and multimodal visualisation technologies are not yet sufficiently advanced or robust, requiring further research to achieve reliable quantification.
barriers.justification: Technical limitations of sensors and displays constrained the fidelity of prototypes and the team's ability to produce high‑fidelity solutions and fully evaluate them, impacting iteration and implementation planning.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Measuring the human ergonomics demands advancement in sensory technologies and multimodal visualisation displays. Thus, more research is needed in this domain to guide future researchers and developers towards robust and reliable quantiﬁcation techniques.

barriers.description: Physical design issues were reported by participants (glove size for small hands, left‑handedness, and exposure of electronics to patient skin), indicating the prototype did not fully meet diverse user requirements.
barriers.justification: These usability and safety concerns limited the team's ability to satisfy user requirements and produce an unintrusive, inclusive design, thereby constraining further iteration and wider user testing.
barriers.reference_excerpt: In particular, the following concerns raised among the answers; Paying attention to the patient’s face during familiarisation stage, glove size for small hands and left handedness, exposure of the electronics to patient’s skin.
